drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. A retailer routes about two million customer emails a day
drills.answer_line: SAM: The answer is B: test the smallest, fastest tier
drills.stem: A retailer routes about two million emails a day into twelve queues. Each decision must return in under a second, the budget is tight, and an eval set defines acceptable accuracy. The prototype's largest model at high effort is too slow and too expensive. What is the best approach?

options.A: Keep the largest model and turn on fast mode
options.B: Test the smallest, fastest tier on the eval set; adopt it if it meets the bar
options.C: Keep the largest model at maximum effort for accuracy headroom
options.D: Move to the middle tier and lengthen the prompt with every edge case

drills.why: High-volume, latency-sensitive classification is the documented Haiku use case, gated by the eval. Fast mode adds premium price to a cost-constrained job.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A team's regression test sends a fixed prompt
drills.answer_line: SAM: But the documentation does not promise determinism at any setting
drills.stem: A regression test asserts that the reply to a fixed prompt equals a stored string exactly. Temperature is zero. The test fails on about one run in ten with no code change. What is the best fix?

options.A: Also set top_k to 1 so only the most likely token is chosen
options.B: Assert on properties that matter, such as schema validity and required fields, over several runs
options.C: Switch to a larger model, which is more consistent
options.D: Retry the call until the output matches the stored string

drills.why: Even at temperature 0, output is not fully deterministic. Design for variation: check structure and meaning, not bytes.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A chat assistant runs a large model
drills.scenario: Long wait before the first word
drills.stem: Choose two. A chat assistant runs a large model at high effort with adaptive thinking. Users complain about a long wait before the first word appears on simple questions. Which two changes most directly shorten the time to the first visible text?

options.A: Lower effort for this route so simple questions skip most thinking
options.B: Stream the response so text appears as it is generated
options.E: Add five worked examples to the system prompt

drills.why: Fast mode raises output tokens per second, not time to first token. Less thinking and streaming shorten the wait before the first word.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. For each statement, say true or false.
drills.prompt: True or false: (1) effort affects only thinking, not text or tool calls; (2) max_tokens caps thinking and response together; (3) thinking tokens bill as output tokens; (4) fast mode runs a smaller model.
drills.answer: 1 false (effort affects every output token); 2 true; 3 true; 4 false (same model, faster inference configuration).

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. An invoice extraction prompt includes one worked example
drills.answer_line: ALEX: A. B is louder guidance
drills.stem: An invoice extraction prompt has one worked example, an invoice in euros. On invoices in other currencies, the output sometimes reports euros anyway. What is the best fix?

options.A: Add 3-5 diverse examples in <example> tags covering several currencies and layouts
options.B: Add "IMPORTANT: use the invoice's own currency" in capitals
options.C: Remove the example and go zero-shot
options.D: Raise the temperature so the model explores other currencies

drills.why: One example is a template the model copies. Diverse examples show which features vary.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A team moves its service to a newer model I D.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: C. A four hundred is a request
drills.scenario: Prefill breaks on a newer model
drills.stem: After moving to a newer model ID, every request that starts the assistant's reply with an opening brace, to force JSON, returns a 400 error. What is the best fix?

options.A: Return to the old model permanently
options.B: Retry the failing requests with backoff
options.C: Remove the prefill and request the JSON shape through structured outputs

drills.why: Prefill is rejected on newer models. A 400 is not transient, so retrying changes nothing; the old model will retire.

drills.question_line: SAM: Recall first. Pause and name the four segments, and the giveaway for each.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: How a model writes: exact-match tests fail.
drills.prompt: Name the four segments, and the giveaway for each.
drills.answer: How a model writes: exact-match tests fail. Thinking, effort and speed: which wait the user means. Shots: outputs copy the example. Choosing a model: the quality bar, latency and volume.
